THE SOLACE OF THE BLIND
If all the residents of New South Wales were to shut their eyes and keep them shut resolutely for even 20 minutes, the Industrial Blind Institution would not need to appeal for funds.
Now, what about it? The Institution asks for help to enable it to carry on the good work of making the blind self-supporting.

This institution is not a "charity"; it is a philanthropic business undertaking. At the last annual meeting the chairman, Sir A. W. Meeks, M.L.C., stressed this point, and said: "We help the blind to help themselves."
The various departments of the institution are run on regular factory lines; the men and women are well paid for their labor, and the work is amazingly well done.
Place an order for a chair, brushes, or cocoon matting, and you will find that the article turned out by the "seeing fingers" will compare with any product made by workmen who have seeing eyes.
But, good as are the teachers, and industrious as are the pupils, such an in-
Industry cannot compete financially with those run by commercial men for profit, so that last year the manufacturing department showed a loss of £850.

But against that is the gain to the men and women who would otherwise be incapable of earning anything, and must become, through their unmerited misfortune, objects of casual charity or burdens on their families.

The wages earned by the blind in the institution last year amounted to £5055. In addition to this, certain allowances made over and above the award paid for piece-workers accounted for another £2388. The sales of manufactured goods realised £16,622, which is evidence of the great amount of work done by the 122 blind workers.

The expenses of the institution are very heavy. Here are just a few examples of how the money goes, taken from the last balance-sheet: Home for blind women £641/18/8, medical attendance and sick pay £448/4/2, instructors' wages £618, pianos and musical instruments £109 17/4, additions to workshops £3566/19/11.

The building at the foot of William-street hums with activity. To feel the tragedy of those who are working inside the visitor should walk across Hyde Park and realise that none of these cheerful men and women, who are turning out technically perfect articles, can see the wonder of the flowers and trees just outside.

Yet they are as happy yet humans may be. One would say offhand that all the doormats in Sydney must be made at the institution, so busy are the men in this department—some at looms, some getting the cord ready, and some finishing the itch.
Hundreds of yards of cocoanut matting are being turned out on the big looms, and it is remarkable how the blind评估 at once turns to fix a loom that has slipped out of its rope hangings.

In its desire to bring comforts within the reach of its works, the institution has established a wholesale grocery shop. This is conducted by voluntary help. An attractive range of goods is stocked and sold at exactly the prices paid by the management.

Farewell Concert By the Conservatorium Orchestra
Saturday, December 27th, 1919
Henri Verbrugghen
Director of the N.S.W. State Conservatorium of Music and Conductor of its Orchestra

Henri Verbrugghen, the only child of a Belgian merchant, was born at Brussels in 1873. His early training was undertaken by his mother, a lady whose devotion to Beethoven and whose charm of personality attracted to the home the lovers of Chamber Music, a branch whose study her son has never ceased to pursue ardently. Despite the success of his first public appearance as a Violinist when 8 years of age, it was intended that he should adopt medicine as a profession. However, on the advice of Joseph Wieniawski and M. Gevaert, the distinguished classicist and Director of the Brussels Conservatoire, this resolve was departed from, and at the age of thirteen he entered the Conservatoire as a student, first under Hubay, and thereafter under Ysaye, whose favourite pupil he soon became. In his final triumph against all competitors in 1889, the predictions of the press at the time of his early prize-winning found ample fulfillment. Upon the advice of M. Gevaert, young Verbrugghen, then sixteen years old, assiduously applied himself to the study of Orchestration and Instrumentation, and gained admission to the Society of Conservatoire Concerts, an Orchestra d'elite in which Ysaye, Caesar Thomson and all the teachers of the Conservatoire took part in the performance of the masterpieces. In order to extend his knowledge of symphonic music he became a first violin in the Scottish Orchestra on its foundation under Henschel in 1893; and during the following winter he accepted a similar post under Lamoureux, in Paris, where he also had an opportunity of joining Professor Delsart in quartet playing. During the summer of the same year he acted as leader to Jules Riviere at Llandudno. Here also, as Deputy Conductor for three successive summers, he gained his first experience in conducting, realising thereby that in the attainment of proficiency in this branch lay his true vocation. But the period when he had full scope for the development of his skill and the extension of his technical equipment as a Conductor was during his four years' Directorship of Music at Colwyn Bay. At the time of leaving for New South Wales, Mr. Verbrugghen had engagements for upwards of 80 Orchestral Concerts in London and the Provinces. His selection as Director of the New South Wales Conservatorium was made before the war, from worldwide applications by a London Committee composed of the chief musicians of Great Britain, and also by the Conservatorium Council in Sydney, acting independently, and there is scarcely a man, who, through his experience and practical achievements, is better qualified and offers more guarantees for the success of the Institution on sound practical and artistic lines. At the end of 1917, Mr. Verbrugghen paid a visit to America with the object of inquiring into the methods of the music schools in the United States. His reputation as an orchestral conductor having preceded him to New York, he was the recipient of several offers for his services, but owing to the shortness of his stay, he was able to make only one appearance. This was with the Russian Symphony Orchestra. Mr. Verbrugghen's London and Sydney successes were paralleled by this performance, as was gathered from the comments in the musical columns of the New York daily press.
W. KNIBB, Viola.

A sectional committee formed to draw up a scheme for a Conservatorium of Music, on 18th July, 1912, finally adopted a report to the full committee. That report placed on record the high appreciation expressed by the Committee of the Minister's efforts to bring to a head at last 'this long debated project.' The report continued, 'The art community of this country has reached a stage of development which assures to any properly established Conservatorium an immense influence for good. The musical community of the State may fairly be described as one in which, while the raw material of art instinct and art ability is abundantly available, there is a lack of standards and an absence of authoritative influences towards them.' Another paragraph of the report is prophetic. It is as follows:- 'Into the confusion of defective standards and the bewilderment of an art community striving eagerly enough, but also hopelessly enough, to discern what is best, such an institution would come with all the force of authority. It would demonstrate the truth of things. It would dissipate the wrong ideas of musical art which fill this country, and in their place would set up right ideas.' It was therefore urged that the Conservatorium be established on an impressive scale, and that it should not be, in any sense of the term, 'a hole and corner affair.' It was urged that the institution he housed with all the dignity befitting a great undertaking, and that the Director be appointed from a world range of candidature. A preference was expressed for a Director of ability in Opera and Orchestra. In this regard the Committee expressed the opinion that 'an orchestra is an essential need of any community hoping for musical progress.' Appendices to the report set out a series of resolutions adopted by the Committee and a financial statement of the proposed institution.

The Minister for Education, the Hon. Campbell Carmichael, was in London at the time applications closed, and availed himself of the opportunity of conferring with members of the Selection Committee. The result was the selection of Mr. Henri Verbrugghen. It is interesting at this stage to recall the opinion expressed by one of the Selection Committee in regard to Mr. Verbrugghen. The outbreak of the Great War made it necessary to defer action, consequently it was not till early in 1915 that Mr. Verbrugghen was invited to accept the position of Director, and in August, 1915, he entered on duty.

In the meantime the vexed question of whether the old Government House Stables should be converted into a restaurant or a Conservatorium of Music was settled—in this case art proving triumphant. The building work was proceeded with and in May, 1915, the Inaugural Concert was held.

The first Orchestral Concert under the Director was given on April 8th, 1916, to a full and enthusiastic audience. On July 5th, the second concert took place with an unmistakable gain in technical accomplishments, powers of expression, style, finish and quality of tone. The press, speaking of this concert, said:—
E. STEELE, Violin.

Then came the glorious 1919 with the momentous advent of the State Orchestra. Mr. Verbrugghen had proved to the Government and to the public that it was possible to organise successfully a first-class orchestra, and so he was able to bring about the consummation of his plans, and it is much to the credit of the New South Wales Government that they have made it possible for the Director and the State Orchestra to give the splendid series of concerts which has made 1919 memorable in the annals of our musical activities.

N. INGAMELLS,
Bassoon.

"Those who attend these concerts are witnesses to the working of magic. Beautiful, naturally, and so unobtrusively, a great symphony orchestra is coming into existence under their very eyes. . . . . . We declare frankly that the State is wonderfully fortunate to have secured the services of a splendid artist like Mr. Henri Verbrugghen, a man of great musical learning, of extraordinary striving always towards the consummation of the noblest things in the divine art of music. Even in these few short months of effort he has done signal things with his String Quartet, and with his latest orchestral concert he has gained fresh laurels. . . . With Beethoven's Second Symphony, the music grew more intense, more heroic. . . . In such interpretation as Mr. Verbrugghen's, we realise this greatness in the grandest of all the grand masters."
The third concert was held on Saturday, 4th November, and the "Sun" expressed itself as follows:—
Miss M. SMITH, Violin.
"The afternoon was full of interest, and everywhere there was ample evidence of how rapidly Mr. Verbrugghen is bringing into life a really valuable symphony orchestra."
The "Daily Telegraph" of the same concert remarks:—

"The great artistic attraction and educational influence of the Orchestra are becoming better known. . . . . Such music in these days of[tumult makes for renewal of serenity and sanity. In the midst of their titanic struggles we are told that the Germans throng their concert rooms, and we need not have a less living faith in the refreshing and fortifying power of music. From this point of view one would welcome a weekly concert by the Verbruggen Orchestra. A consummation indeed devoutly to be wished, but difficult of realisation unless some music loving billionaire, as in Boston, Chicago, New York, and St. Louis, comes forward with the necessary financial endowment."

And these concerts actually paid for themselves.

It is anticipated that the year will terminate with £2000 profit, and probably more, but it must remembered that the Orchestra has been free from all burden as regards the salary of a conductor, as Mr. Verbrugghen has not claimed the slightest remuneration for all his labour. It is a matter of common knowledge that in America the conductors of large orchestras receive from £3000 to £6000 for a season of seven months. It will be remembered that overtures were made to secure the services of Mr. Verbrugghen for one of the large American Organestras at a salary of £5000 for a seven months' engagement shortly after his return from America.

Towards this grand work the State has already done its duty, and the public has awakened to its responsibility, and shown appreciation of the efforts put forth.

Intense enthusiasm prevailed, and in Melbourne the success was so marked that nothing will now satisfy the musicians of the Southern Capital but a State orchestra of their own.

Finally, let us lavish all praise upon our State Orchestra, but let us not forget that after all it is the Conservatorium Orchestra, and that without the Conservatorium its establishment would still have been a problem for the future to solve.

In the first variation the strings play the theme pizzicato, over which runs a counterpoint for flutes and clarinets. The second variation is a rapid bravura for all the violins in the manner of a moto continuuo. Variation three is for the wood-wind alone, without oboes. The sixth variation is a very much quickened version of the theme by 'cellos and violas, accompanied by detached chords from the rest of the orchestra. Variation seven is a simple statement of the theme for wood-wind only, and leads to the eighth variation, which is a solo for cor anglais, in A Minor—largo—accompanied by strings in the high register tremolando. The ninth variation is gay and piquant, with an exciting termination; at the sudden stop, a cadenza for solo violin joins on to the tenth variation which is a violin solo in B Minor, in the style of a slow waltz, accompanied by strings pizzicato. The 11th variation is in B Major, for strings, wood-wind and horns, ending ritenuto for the basses leading to the 12th variation—Finale—tempo di polacca, the whole work being a fine example of the genius which can invest a simple theme with infinite variety and colour.

Schubert had here left incomplete a work which, for its nameless charm and its power over the listener, is undoubtedly his finest and most characteristic orchestral composition. A recent writer says concerning this symphony: "‘In general, it is assuredly unfortunate when an author does not finish his work, but of this symphony I might almost say it is fortunate that it remained uncompleted. The first movement is full of a tragic grandeur that, apart from Beethoven, no other symphonist has been able to attain. I consider that subject given out by the 'cellos as one of the most beautiful inspirations it has ever been given to a musician to express. That which in the first movement gives us the vivid impression of a soul-struggle, seems in the second movement an ideal gentleness, as if the musician was already planning his journey towards eternal rest. For my part, this ending is so satisfying that I have never had, after the second movement, the desire to hear a continuation of the work. By the breadth and force of sentiment, united to the tenderly lyricic element, which flits across his work like a ray of light, Schubert appears a noble and somewhat feminine complement of Beethoven.'

Musicians regard the Unfinished Symphony as Schubert's most individual creation; one of his biographers looks upon it as a parable in sound of the composer's own life, typifying the brief but glamorous career, abruptly terminated just when its promises were being fulfilled. The passages, so purely and melodiously beautiful, leading by sudden transitions to others of a wild and agitated character, illustrate with sad fidelity the gleams of happiness which occasionally illustrate Schubert's path, only to be followed by a renewal of darkness and failure. Critics, with a natural and pardonable impulse, have endeavoured to prove that this music is a true picture of the composer's mind at the time of writing.

"The marvellous profusion of gifts that combined to make up the musical genius of Franz Schubert asserts itself nowhere more conspicuously than in the two movements known as the "Unfinished Symphony." Listening to them, however, with the knowledge that their composer had not completed his twenty-sixth year when he put them to paper, excites not only our wonder, but also, in an exceptional degree, our sympathy, for these strains reveal an intimacy with the accents of suffering that could only have been purchased by experience. Suffering is, however, the price which Nature exacts for the most precious of her revelations."

Schubert, short as was his life, lived six years after writing the first two movements of this symphony, so that there is, apparently, no reason why he should not have finished the work. That he intended to do so is proved by the fact that he wrote a few bars of the third movement. Why, after this, he abandoned the symphony has remained a mystery.

We have spoken of the accents-of despair—of despair, it might be said—that are so prominent in this work. Note the gloomy horror-stricken phrase for 'cello and basses with which the work opens, and which might well stand for a musical embodiment of Dante's awful line, "All hope abandon, ye who enter here," and one's flesh positively creeps at the shuddering figure of the strings, that ushers in and accompanies theoidal first subject.

The tragic note is, of course, not maintained throughout. Witness the soothing 'second subject,' which is ushered in by the bass, and might be a cradle-song so restful is the rhythm—a complete contrast to the first, and is all beauty and tender sentiment. This new subject is first given out by the 'cellos, violas and clarionets accompanying in syncophated notes. Next it is taken up by the violins in octaves, and is heard again and again, interrupted by savage bursts of wild modulations, through which its artillery simplicity remains unimpaired. Again the original mysterious passage for the basses is heard, and with it begins the working out of this movement, which is a marvel for the touching contrast in the attenuation of tones, so deeply pathetic, so unaffected, so guileless, with the wild, gloomy, furious outburst which powerfully affect all earnest listeners and students of this music. This wonderful movement is concluded by four sullen chords.
